artworks.title: Pygmalion and Galatea
artworks.description: Girodet's Louvre canvas catches the ivory maiden as flesh: Cupid's torch lights the statue-bride while Pygmalion kneels. Ovid never names her Galatea, but reception made the living ivory the Galatea of the salon.

artworks.title: Pygmalion Praying Venus to Animate His Statue
artworks.description: Regnault's Origin of Sculpture: the ivory virgin still on her pedestal while Pygmalion begs Venus for life — the bride before the kiss that will make her mother of Paphos.

artworks.title: Pygmalion and Galatea
artworks.description: Gérôme's academic kiss: marble softens from the lips downward as the sculptor's bride comes alive — the definitive modern image of the ivory maiden.

artworks.title: Pygmalion and the Image: The Soul Attains
artworks.description: Burne-Jones' final Birmingham panel: the image steps living from the pedestal into Pygmalion's arms — the soul attained, the statue become bride.

music.title: Pigmalion
music.description: Rameau's acte de ballet ends with the statue stepping down alive — the ivory bride as the climax of French baroque metamorphosis.

popCulture.title: Metamorphoses
popCulture.creator: Ovid
popCulture.description: Book 10: the unnamed ivory virgin Venus warms to life — mother of Paphos, the Cypriot eponym, and the root of every later Galatea.

popCulture.title: Galatea (video game)
popCulture.creator: Emily Short
popCulture.description: Short's interactive fiction puts the player opposite the living statue — Galatea answering from the pedestal in a landmark of IF conversation.

popCulture.title: Galatea
popCulture.description: Later tradition names Pygmalion's bride Galatea — carefully distinct from Galatea the Nereid beloved of Acis.
